name: Spheroidal Stars
description: Static fluid spheres with spheroidal and paraboloidal spatial geometries.
convention: We use areal coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\phi)$, with $t$ a time and $r$ a length. Components use $x^0=ct$, with factors of $c$ explicit in the line element. The constant $C$ has dimensions of inverse squared length, and $r_b$ is the surface radius.
history: P. C. Vaidya and Ramesh Tikekar built their 1982 star on a spheroid in four dimensional Euclidean space [vaidya1982spheroid, khugaev2016]. The fluid is static and spherically symmetric, while the spatial curvature varies with distance from the centre. Two principal radii of the spheroid determine the radial metric, and their ratio determines how the density falls outward [khugaev2016]. Equality of the radial and tangential pressures fixes a differential equation for the gravitational redshift [khugaev2016, thirukkanesh2009].¶Hans A. Buchdahl had introduced the same rational form of the radial metric in 1959 [buchdahl1959, khugaev2016]. Vaidya and Tikekar's original star has $K=+2$ for $g_{rr}=(1+Kr^2/L^2)/(1-r^2/L^2)$, with $L$ a constant length; the convention $g_{rr}=(1-Kr^2/L^2)/(1-r^2/L^2)$ assigns it $K=-2$ [khugaev2016]. This is also the finite fluid sphere that M. C. Durgapal and R. Bannerji obtained in 1983, identified by M. S. R. Delgaty and Kayll Lake with Buchdahl's 1959 solution [durgapal1983bannerji, delgaty1998]. Its lapse combines $(1+x)^{3/2}$ and $(5+2x)\sqrt{2-x}$, where $x=2r^2/L^2$, and its density remains finite at the centre [thirukkanesh2009].¶Durgapal chose the time component first in August 1982, setting $g_{tt}=-a^2(1+Cr^2)^n$, with $C$ a positive inverse squared length and $a$ a normalization of time [durgapal1982]. An integer exponent $n$ makes the remaining equation exactly integrable [durgapal1982]. The first power is Tolman IV, and the second is Wyman IIa with its parameter equal to one [delgaty1998]. The third is H. Heintzmann's solution IIa of 1969 [delgaty1998]. Durgapal IV and V, with $n=4$ and $n=5$, have decreasing density and pressure and a sound speed below that of light for suitable choices of their constants [durgapal1982, delgaty1998].¶M. R. Finch and J. E. F. Skea integrated the pressure equation for $g_{rr}=1+Cr^2$ in 1989 [finch1989, delgaty1998]. Their lapse contains sines and cosines of $\sqrt{1+Cr^2}$, multiplied by expressions linear in that same square root [thirukkanesh2009]. The density is $8\pi G\epsilon/c^4=C(3+Cr^2)/(1+Cr^2)^2$, with $\epsilon$ the energy density, so it is finite at the centre and decreases outward [thirukkanesh2009]. The ratio of its lapse constants fixes the pressure profile; matching the lapse to Schwarzschild's exterior fixes the normalization of time [thirukkanesh2009, delgaty1998].¶A regular centre and a surface with zero pressure restrict every one of these stars. Delgaty and Lake checked these conditions in 1998, together with pressure isotropy, positive central density and pressure, decreasing matter profiles, and a sound speed below that of light [delgaty1998]. Buchdahl's finite sphere, Durgapal IV and V, and Finch and Skea's star passed their tests for specific parameter choices [delgaty1998]. At the surface the fluid matches Schwarzschild's vacuum, with the exterior mass fixed by the radial metric and the normalization of time fixed by the lapse [delgaty1998, khugaev2016]. A positive surface density is compatible with this matching because the pressure vanishes there [delgaty1998].

related.text: The equilibrium equations for a static sphere of fluid. Each of these stars satisfies them with its own density and pressure [delgaty1998].
The vacuum outside each star. At the surface the pressure vanishes, and the lapse and radial metric match the exterior of the enclosed mass [delgaty1998].
The star of uniform density. Vaidya and Tikekar's spatial ansatz becomes its spherical spatial geometry at $K=0$ [khugaev2016].
A static fluid sphere whose density falls quadratically with the areal radius. Durgapal IV and V and Finch and Skea's star have different density profiles [delgaty1998].
Buchdahl's fluid sphere of 1964 extends to infinity with a finite mass. His finite star of 1959 is the Vaidya-Tikekar and Durgapal-Bannerji solution [delgaty1998].
